subtopics.name: Discharge planning and continuity of care

questions.stem: At 1500 the nurse on a surgical unit receives four call lights at once. Which client should the nurse see first?

options.text: A client 6 hours after a thyroidectomy who says their voice sounds different and is now making a high-pitched sound when breathing in
A client 1 day after a laparoscopic appendectomy who reports shoulder pain rated 6 of 10 and asks for the prescribed oxycodone dose that is due now
A client 2 days after a bowel resection whose nasogastric tube has drained 200 mL of green fluid since the start of the shift and who feels nauseated
A client 3 days after a mastectomy who is crying and says the drain makes them afraid to look at the incision

rationale.correct: Use the ABCs: stridor after neck surgery threatens the airway and comes before expected pain, expected drainage and emotional needs.

perOption.a: Stridor after thyroid surgery can mean airway swelling, bleeding into the neck or laryngeal nerve injury; the airway is at risk.
perOption.b: Shoulder pain after laparoscopy is usually from the gas used in surgery and is expected; pain medicine can follow.
perOption.c: Green gastric drainage of this amount is expected; nausea needs attention after the airway problem.
perOption.d: Emotional support is important, but it comes after the client whose airway is threatened.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize a threatened airway after thyroid surgery.

questions.stem: In a long-term care facility, the RN works with a licensed practical nurse (LPN). Which task should the RN keep rather than assign to the LPN?

options.text: Giving scheduled insulin to a resident with stable type 2 diabetes whose glucose has stayed in range for the past week
Assessing a resident who returned from the hospital today with a new stage 3 pressure injury and new medications
Reinforcing the inhaler teaching the RN gave last week to a resident with COPD who is ready to practice again
Giving crushed medications through the feeding tube of a resident with a stroke who has had the tube for months

rationale.correct: The RN keeps initial and changed-condition assessments, care planning and evaluation; the LPN gives care to stable residents with predictable needs.

perOption.a: Giving medications to stable residents is within the LPN's scope.
perOption.b: The initial assessment of a resident whose condition and plan have changed is the RN's responsibility.
perOption.c: Reinforcing teaching the RN has already given is within the LPN's scope.
perOption.d: Giving medications through an established tube is within the LPN's scope.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Decide which tasks the RN keeps.

questions.stem: The intensive care unit is full, and two critically ill clients are waiting in the emergency department. The charge nurse must choose 2 clients who can safely transfer to the medical unit. Which 2 clients should the charge nurse choose?

options.text: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis whose anion gap closed 12 hours ago and who now takes subcutaneous insulin and eats meals
A client 6 hours after a large stroke who is receiving a nicardipine infusion to keep the blood pressure in range
A client with pneumonia who was extubated 36 hours ago and has an SpO2 of 95% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula
A client with septic shock who started norepinephrine 4 hours ago and has a lactate of 4.1 mmol/L
A client with an acute GI bleed who received 3 units of blood today and whose hemoglobin is still falling

rationale.correct: Transfer out of intensive care the clients who are stable on routine treatments, and keep those on titrated infusions or with ongoing instability.

perOption.a: DKA has resolved and the client is on a routine regimen that a medical unit can manage.
perOption.b: A titrated vasoactive infusion and an early unstable stroke need ICU monitoring.
perOption.c: The client has been stable off the ventilator for over a day on low-flow oxygen.
perOption.d: Active shock on a vasopressor needs intensive care.
perOption.e: Ongoing bleeding with a falling hemoglobin is unstable.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose clients for transfer when beds are short.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel (AP) tells the nurse at 1100 that all of the morning vital signs are done and charted. While reviewing the chart, the nurse sees that one client's temperature was 38.9 °C (102 °F) at 0800, which the AP did not report. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Talk with the AP privately about which findings need to be reported right away, then document the conversation
Assess the client with the fever and notify the provider of the findings
Ask the charge nurse to give the AP a different, lighter assignment for the rest of the shift
Complete an incident report about the delayed reporting and give it to the nurse manager

rationale.correct: When delegated data show a problem, care for the client first, then give feedback to the AP about what must be reported and when.

perOption.a: Clear expectations are needed, but the client with a high fever must be seen first.
perOption.b: The client's safety comes first; the nurse assesses and reports the fever, then follows up with the AP.
perOption.c: Reassigning the AP does not address the client who needs assessment.
perOption.d: Reporting may follow, but it does not help the client now.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Follow up on information missed by assistive personnel.

questions.stem: Which client is legally able to give their own consent for surgery without a parent or guardian?

options.text: A 17-year-old who is a high school senior, lives with their parents and has a part-time job
A 16-year-old who is married and lives with their spouse in their own apartment
A 15-year-old who is visiting grandparents and has the grandparents' permission
A 17-year-old whose parents are away and who says they will agree to it later by phone

rationale.correct: Emancipated minors (for example married, in the military, or legally emancipated) can consent to their own care; other minors need a parent or guardian except for specific services.

perOption.a: A minor who lives with and depends on their parents usually needs a parent's consent for surgery.
perOption.b: Married minors are generally treated as emancipated and can consent to their own care.
perOption.c: Grandparents are not legal guardians unless appointed; the parent must consent.
perOption.d: A minor cannot consent alone; the nurse must reach a parent for consent.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify who can give consent.

questions.stem: A client with early Parkinson's disease asks the nurse, "What's the difference between a living will and a health care power of attorney?" Which response is accurate?

options.text: "A living will names the person who decides for you, and a power of attorney lists the treatments you want."
"A living will states the treatments you want or refuse, and a power of attorney names someone to decide if you can't."
"They are the same document, and either one lets your family make financial and medical decisions for you."
"These documents can be signed by your family once you have lost the ability to make your own decisions about treatment."

rationale.correct: A living will records treatment wishes; a durable power of attorney for health care names a person to make decisions when the client cannot.

perOption.a: This reverses the two documents.
perOption.b: A living will gives written treatment wishes; a health care power of attorney appoints an agent to make decisions.
perOption.c: They are different, and neither is a financial power of attorney.
perOption.d: The client signs them while able to make decisions.

questions.educationalObjective: Explain types of advance directives.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with a spiral fracture of the femur. The parent says the child fell off a couch onto a carpeted floor. The nurse also notes healing bruises on the child's back and buttocks. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the parent to explain how each of the bruises happened before reporting anything
Report the suspected abuse to child protective services as the law requires
Wait for the provider to examine the child and decide whether abuse is likely
Note the bruises in the record and plan to review the case at the next follow-up visit

rationale.correct: An injury that does not match the story, such as a spiral femur fracture from a short fall in a toddler, with bruises of different ages, must be reported as suspected abuse.

perOption.a: Questioning the parent like an investigator can raise risk to the child; the nurse's duty is to report suspicion.
perOption.b: Nurses are mandated reporters; a reasonable suspicion is enough, and proof is not required.
perOption.c: Every mandated reporter must report reasonable suspicion; the nurse cannot pass the duty to another person.
perOption.d: Delaying the report may leave the child in danger.

questions.educationalObjective: Report suspected child abuse.

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with HIV asks the nurse not to tell their partner. The partner is at the bedside and asks the nurse, "Is it something I could catch?" What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the partner the diagnosis, since the partner has a right to know about the risk
Say that the nurse cannot share the client's health information, and tell the provider
Tell the partner the client has an infection and that the partner should get tested soon
Tell the partner that nothing is wrong so that the client's privacy stays fully protected

rationale.correct: HIV status is protected information. Encourage the client to disclose, and involve the provider and public health partner-notification services.

perOption.a: The nurse cannot disclose the diagnosis without the client's permission.
perOption.b: The nurse protects confidentiality; the provider and public health partner-notification services can help the client inform partners.
perOption.c: Hinting at the diagnosis is still a breach of confidentiality.
perOption.d: The nurse should not give false information.

questions.educationalObjective: Protect confidentiality about HIV status.

questions.stem: A case manager has worked with a client with COPD who was admitted five times last year. Which outcome best shows the case management plan is working?

options.text: The client has learned the names of each of the inhalers they use
The client has had no hospital admissions in the 6 months since the plan began
The client has agreed to attend a pulmonary rehabilitation program next spring
The client's family has visited the hospital less often over the last few months

rationale.correct: Case management aims at better outcomes and lower costs, such as fewer readmissions and emergency visits.

perOption.a: Knowing the names is useful but does not show better outcomes.
perOption.b: Fewer readmissions is the main outcome that shows coordinated care is working.
perOption.c: Agreeing to a program is a step, not an outcome.
perOption.d: Fewer family visits does not measure the client's health.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Evaluate case management outcomes.

questions.stem: During an emergency, the provider gives the nurse a verbal prescription for a medication. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Read the prescription back to the provider
Enter the prescription in the record for the provider to sign
Write down the prescription as it is given
Get the provider's confirmation that it is correct

rationale.correct: Verbal and telephone prescriptions: write down, read back, get confirmation, document and have the prescriber authenticate it.

perOption.a: Writing it down at once avoids relying on memory.
perOption.b: Read-back catches errors in hearing or writing.
perOption.c: The provider confirms the read-back.
perOption.d: Verbal prescriptions are signed by the provider within the time policy allows.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Take a verbal prescription safely.

questions.stem: A nurse's neighbor is admitted to another unit of the hospital. The nurse has access to the electronic health record for work. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Look up the neighbor's test results quickly so the nurse can offer support
Leave the neighbor's record closed, since the nurse is not involved in their care
Ask a coworker who works on the other unit to share how the neighbor is doing today
Read the record but avoid printing, copying or sharing anything that is written in it

rationale.correct: Access client records only when needed for your work; curiosity or friendship is not a reason.

perOption.a: Opening a record without a work reason is a privacy breach, even with good intentions.
perOption.b: Staff may open only the records they need for their job.
perOption.c: Asking others to share protected information is also a breach.
perOption.d: Simply viewing the record without a work reason is a breach.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respect access limits in the health record.

questions.stem: A medical unit is working to reduce its catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) rate. Which piece of data is an outcome measure?

options.text: The percentage of catheters with a documented daily review of whether they are still needed
The number of CAUTIs per 1,000 catheter days on the unit this quarter
The number of staff who completed the catheter insertion training module
The percentage of drainage bags found hanging below the bladder during audits

rationale.correct: Outcome measures show the result for clients (such as infection rates); process measures show whether care steps are done; structure measures show resources such as training.

perOption.a: This is a process measure: it shows whether staff carry out a step.
perOption.b: The infection rate is the outcome the project is trying to change.
perOption.c: Training completion is a structure or process measure.
perOption.d: This is a process measure of care practice.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish outcome measures from process measures.

questions.stem: A nurse educator is reviewing legal issues with nursing staff. For each action, indicate the legal wrong it is most likely to be.

rows.text: Starting an IV on a competent client who refused it
Keeping a competent client from leaving by locking the door
Telling visitors that a coworker is a drunk who should lose their license
Taking a photo of a client's wound and sharing it without consent

rationale.correct: Battery: touching without consent. False imprisonment: unlawful confinement. Defamation: false, damaging statements. Invasion of privacy: sharing private information or images without consent.

perOption.r1:c1: Touching a client without consent is battery.
perOption.r1:c3: Nothing false was said about anyone.
perOption.r2:c2: Confining a competent client against their will is false imprisonment.
perOption.r3:c3: Spreading a false, damaging statement about someone is defamation.
perOption.r3:c4: This is about a coworker's reputation, not client information.
perOption.r4:c3: The photo is not a false statement.
perOption.r4:c4: Sharing a client's image without consent invades privacy.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.educationalObjective: Identify legal wrongs in nursing practice.

questions.stem: A new graduate nurse tells the nurse manager that an experienced nurse often rolls their eyes, criticizes the new nurse in front of clients and leaves them out of breaks. What should the manager do first?

options.text: Tell the new graduate that experienced nurses are often hard on new staff and it will pass
Meet privately with the experienced nurse, describe the behavior and state the expected conduct
Move the new graduate to a different shift so they no longer work with the experienced nurse
Hold a unit meeting and describe the incidents so that the whole staff knows what happened

rationale.correct: Incivility and bullying are addressed promptly and privately, with clear expectations and follow-up under facility policy.

perOption.a: This dismisses bullying, which harms staff and client safety.
perOption.b: Addressing incivility directly and promptly, with clear expectations, is the first step under most workplace policies.
perOption.c: Moving the target of bullying punishes them and leaves the behavior unaddressed.
perOption.d: Discussing one person's behavior in public is unprofessional and may breach confidentiality.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to workplace incivility.

questions.stem: The unit has one infusion pump left, and four clients have new IV prescriptions. Which client should receive the pump?

options.text: A client with a deep vein thrombosis who is starting a weight-based heparin infusion
A client with dehydration who is prescribed 0.9% sodium chloride at 100 mL/hr for 8 hours
A client with cellulitis who is prescribed an IV antibiotic piggyback over 30 minutes three times a day
A client with a peripheral IV that needs to be kept open at a slow rate between doses

rationale.correct: When equipment is limited, use it where precise control matters most, such as high-alert infusions like heparin, insulin or vasoactive drugs.

perOption.a: Heparin is a high-alert medication whose rate must be exact; it needs a pump.
perOption.b: Maintenance saline can be run by gravity with careful monitoring if needed.
perOption.c: An intermittent antibiotic can be given by gravity and monitored for its short run time.
perOption.d: The line can be saline-locked instead of running continuously.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Allocate scarce equipment.

questions.stem: The nurse is giving a handoff report for a client who is being transferred from the emergency department to a medical unit. Which information should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: The client's code status
Allergies and reactions
Laboratory results that are still pending
The nurse's opinion that the client's family is difficult
The time and dose of the last pain medication given
A list of every client the emergency department saw this shift

rationale.correct: A safe handoff includes code status, allergies, recent medications, pending results and current concerns, without personal opinions or other clients' details.

perOption.a: Code status must be known in case of an emergency.
perOption.b: Allergies prevent harmful medication errors.
perOption.c: Pending results need follow-up by the receiving nurse.
perOption.d: Personal opinions are not part of a professional handoff.
perOption.e: This guides safe timing of the next dose.
perOption.f: Other clients' information is not relevant and breaches privacy.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Give a complete handoff report.

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with lymphoma tells the nurse they want a second opinion before starting chemotherapy. The oncologist later tells the nurse this will "just waste time." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the client that the oncologist thinks a second opinion will waste valuable time
Support the client's right to a second opinion and help arrange the referral or records
Encourage the client to start treatment now and seek a second opinion later if the first treatment does not work
Stay neutral and leave the client to work out the second opinion with the oncologist

rationale.correct: Clients have the right to a second opinion and to choose their care; the nurse helps them exercise it.

perOption.a: Passing on the provider's frustration may pressure the client and is not advocacy.
perOption.b: Clients have the right to seek other opinions; the nurse advocates for the client's choice.
perOption.c: This overrides the client's right to make an informed choice about care.
perOption.d: Advocacy means actively supporting the client's rights, not stepping back.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Advocate for a client's right to a second opinion.

questions.stem: A client is scheduled to go home today after treatment for a COPD flare. Review the nurse's note and highlight the findings that suggest the client is not ready for discharge.

segments.text: SpO2 is 89% on 2 L/min, the same as the client's baseline at home
could not show the correct steps for using the new inhaler after two teaching sessions
"My home oxygen company hasn't called me back yet."
Walked 30 m (100 ft) in the hall with a walker

rationale.correct: Discharge readiness includes safe self-management, such as inhaler technique, and arranged equipment such as home oxygen.

perOption.s2: This matches the client's known baseline and home oxygen.
perOption.s4: The client cannot yet manage a key treatment safely at home.
perOption.s8: Home oxygen must be arranged before the client leaves.
perOption.s10: This shows adequate mobility for home.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize when a client is not ready for discharge.

questions.stem: A client with metastatic pancreatic cancer is unresponsive and has multiple organ failure. There is no advance directive. The client's adult children insist that "everything be done," including CPR, although the team agrees it would not help. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Follow the family's wishes without discussion, since the client has no advance directive
Ask for a palliative care or ethics consultation to help the family and team discuss goals of care
Write a do-not-resuscitate order in the record, since the team agrees that CPR would not help the client
Tell the family that CPR would be cruel and that the client would not have wanted it

rationale.correct: When families request treatment the team believes will not help, palliative care and ethics consultations support goals-of-care discussions.

perOption.a: The team should still explore goals of care with the family rather than simply proceed.
perOption.b: Consultations support shared decision-making when families request care the team believes will not help.
perOption.c: Nurses do not write DNR orders, and the family must be involved in the discussion.
perOption.d: This assumes the client's wishes and can damage trust.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to requests for treatment that will not help.

questions.stem: A resident with moderate dementia in a long-term care facility has tried to leave the building twice this week and was found at the front door with a coat on. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep the resident in a locked room for the rest of the day
Use a wander-alert bracelet and schedule supervised walks during the day
Give the prescribed as-needed sedative in the afternoon, when the resident usually becomes restless
Tell the resident firmly that they cannot leave the building and remove their coat from the room

rationale.correct: For residents at risk of elopement, use alert systems, supervised activity, routines and redirection rather than restraints.

perOption.a: Confining the resident is a restraint and is not appropriate.
perOption.b: Electronic alerts protect the resident while supervised activity meets the need to move.
perOption.c: Sedation is a chemical restraint and raises fall risk.
perOption.d: Arguing and removing belongings increase agitation.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prevent elopement in dementia.

questions.stem: A parent calls the pediatric clinic and says their 2-year-old swallowed a small button battery from a remote control about 15 minutes ago. The child is breathing normally and playing. What should the nurse tell the parent?

options.text: Watch the child at home and check the stools for the battery over the next few days
Take the child to the emergency department now for an x-ray, without making the child vomit
Give the child a glass of milk and some bread to help push the battery through quickly
Give syrup of ipecac or put a finger down the throat to make the child vomit it up

rationale.correct: A swallowed button battery is an emergency: go to the emergency department at once for imaging; do not induce vomiting.

perOption.a: A button battery stuck in the esophagus can burn through tissue within 2 hours.
perOption.b: A swallowed button battery is an emergency; an x-ray shows where it is, and lodged batteries need urgent removal.
perOption.c: Food does not move a lodged battery and can delay endoscopy; some guidance allows honey only on a doctor's advice.
perOption.d: Inducing vomiting is not recommended and can cause more injury.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a swallowed button battery.

questions.stem: The home health nurse visits an 80-year-old client who lives alone and uses a walker. Which change to the home should the nurse recommend first to reduce fall risk?

options.text: Remove the loose throw rugs in the hallway and bathroom
Paint the walls a brighter color so the rooms feel more cheerful
Move the bed closer to the window so the client can see outside
Buy a new television that is easier to see from across the room

rationale.correct: Home fall prevention: remove loose rugs and clutter, add lighting and night lights, install grab bars and keep often-used items within reach.

perOption.a: Loose rugs are a common cause of trips and falls, especially with a walker.
perOption.b: Paint color does not reduce fall risk.
perOption.c: Bed placement near a window does not address fall hazards.
perOption.d: This does not reduce fall risk.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Reduce fall hazards in the home.

questions.stem: The nurse is observing a new staff member giving injections. Which action requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Activating the safety shield on the needle right after the injection is given
Putting the cap back on a used needle with two hands before walking to the sharps container
Placing the used syringe and needle in a wall-mounted sharps container that is about half full
Taking a portable sharps container into the room to the bedside before giving the injection

rationale.correct: Do not recap used needles; activate safety devices and dispose of sharps right away in a container at the point of use.

perOption.a: Activating the safety device right away prevents needlestick injuries.
perOption.b: Two-handed recapping of used needles causes needlestick injuries and must be avoided.
perOption.c: Sharps containers are used until about three-quarters full.
perOption.d: Keeping the container close reduces the distance a used needle is carried.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prevent needlestick injuries.

questions.stem: A long-term care facility has no private rooms available. A resident has just been found to have MRSA in a draining leg wound. Where should the resident be placed?

options.text: With a resident who has had a recent hip replacement and an open surgical wound
With another resident who also has MRSA and no other infection
With a resident receiving chemotherapy who has a low white blood cell count
With a resident who has Clostridioides difficile diarrhea and is on contact precautions

rationale.correct: If no private room is available, cohort residents with the same organism, and never with residents who are immunosuppressed or have open wounds.

perOption.a: A resident with an open wound is at high risk of infection from MRSA.
perOption.b: When private rooms are not available, cohorting residents with the same organism is acceptable.
perOption.c: An immunosuppressed resident is at high risk of a serious infection.
perOption.d: Residents with different organisms should not share a room.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Make room placements for a resident with MRSA.

questions.stem: On a postpartum unit, which situation requires the nurse to act right away to protect the newborn's security?

options.text: The newborn's identification band matches the parent's band during a check at the bedside
A person in scrubs without a hospital ID badge offers to take the newborn to the nursery
The parent keeps the newborn's crib on the side of the bed away from the door
The newborn's security tag alarms when the nurse carries the baby near the unit exit

rationale.correct: Infant security: matching ID bands, security tags, staff with special ID badges and teaching parents to hand the baby only to verified staff.

perOption.a: Matching bands is correct practice.
perOption.b: Infant abductors often pose as staff; the parent should hand the baby only to staff with the correct ID badge.
perOption.c: Keeping the baby away from the door is a recommended safety measure.
perOption.d: The alarm is working as intended; staff check the reason right away.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Protect newborns from abduction.

testSets.title: NCLEX-RN adaptive exam
testSets.description: Works like the real NCLEX-RN: each question depends on your answers so far, and the exam stops once your result is clear, after 85 to 150 questions. Choose timed (5 hours) or untimed. No going back; answers and rationales at the end. The questions are being rewritten to real NCLEX difficulty and recalibrated, so treat your result as a practice estimate.
